speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: As such, may I propose that the debates on both Bills take place together, although we will still have a formal Second Reading of the Companies and Limited Liability Partnerships (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill to comply with the procedural requirements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Money laundering has been a subject of significant public interest recently, largely due to the $3 billion money laundering case uncovered last year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: While insights from the incident have been incorporated, I would like to emphasise that the proposals in both Bills are part of MOF and ACRA's ongoing enhancements and were in development even before the case was uncovered.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Corporate service providers (CSPs) play an important role in anti-money laundering.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: CSPs provide a range of services to businesses, such as helping them to comply with regulatory requirements, like the filing of annual returns; as well as other services, such as arranging for another person to act as a director of a business.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As CSPs may support companies in a number of key company activities, they serve as gatekeepers against the misuse of companies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They are, therefore, regulated by ACRA to ensure that they fulfil their obligations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Today, non-residents looking to set up companies in Singapore must engage a CSP to do so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: While this is not mandatory for locals, many locals still opt to engage CSPs to facilitate company incorporation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Regardless of whether their clients are Residents or not, all CSPs must conduct customer due diligence before incorporating a company.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This Bill will enhance our regulatory regime for CSPs to deter the misuse of companies and bolster our efforts to combat money laundering.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are three key areas of the CSP Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, all entities carrying on a business in Singapore of providing corporate services must register with ACRA as a CSP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Under the current regime, only CSPs that carry out transactions with ACRA on their customers' behalf are required to register with ACRA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With this Bill, we will expand ACRA's regulatory scope to include Singapore-based entities that provide corporate services, even if they do not transact with ACRA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These could be, for example, entities that provide corporate services exclusively to overseas clients and, hence, do not transact with ACRA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition, we will also extend the obligation to register to include entities that, in relation to their provision of accounting services, carry out specific services defined by the Financial Action Task Force.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The widened coverage of ACRA's regulatory regime will ensure that all entities providing corporate services from Singapore, regardless of whether they serve local or foreign clients, have the same obligations in our fight against financial crime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The second key area of the CSP Bill is the introduction of fines on CSPs and their senior management for non-compliance with their duties to combat financial crime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Today, ACRA already imposes sanctions on CSPs and their registered qualified individuals for non-compliance with ACRA's regulations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These include financial penalties of up to $25,000 per breach, or in egregious scenarios, the suspension or cancellation of their registration.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Since 2021, ACRA has taken an increasingly strict stance over CSPs and registered qualified individuals found to be non-compliant.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Between 2021 and June this year, ACRA has imposed 41 sanctions against CSPs and registered qualified individuals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In 31 of these cases, the registration of the CSPs or registered qualified individuals was cancelled or suspended.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Additionally, the senior management of such firms, such as the chief executive officer (CEO), can, in certain circumstances be held liable for such breaches.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, if they knew or ought reasonably to have known that the offence would be or is being committed, but failed to take all reasonable steps to prevent or stop the commission of that offence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, upon conviction, they can, likewise, be fined up to $100,000.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The third area of the CSP Bill, will address the potential misuse of nominee directorship arrangements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A nominee director is a person who is appointed as a director of a company, but acts according to another person's directions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All directors play an important role in preventing the misuse of companies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They owe fiduciary duties to a company and are required to discharge their duties responsibly, with honesty and reasonable diligence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Nominee directors have the same legal obligations as other directors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Those who fail in discharging their duties can face sanctions, including disqualification and debarment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We recognise that nominee directorship arrangements are a legitimate service provided by many CSPs, to support their overseas-based clients to set up a company in Singapore and fulfil Singapore's requirement for an ordinarily resident director.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, such arrangements are vulnerable to abuse and can lead to the conduct of illicit activities if the nominee directors do not perform their fiduciary duties well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As important gatekeepers in the ecosystem, CSPs cannot arrange for nominee directorships in a cavalier manner.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In some cases, we have observed individuals who are clearly unfit to bear the responsibilities of being a director, but were arranged by errant CSPs to act as nominee directors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will, therefore, do more to tackle the misuse of nominee directorship arrangements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Second, CSPs will be required to ensure that the individuals they arrange to act as nominee directors are fit and proper.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The general principle is that, CSPs must apply their professional judgement and appoint individuals who possess the necessary competencies as nominee directors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: CSPs should also be satisfied with the capacity, conduct and integrity of these individuals, which could include checking their compliance records to evaluate if they have the capacity to take on additional directorships.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are two sets of amendments in this Bill which will help to enhance the transparency of companies and LLPs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first set of amendments will enhance the accuracy of the information contained on the various registers that are currently maintained by companies and LLPs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Today, both companies and LLPs are required to maintain registers of their registrable controllers or beneficial owners.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These are individuals or corporate entities that have a significant interest in or significant control over the company or LLP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition, companies are also required to maintain registers of their nominee directors and nominee shareholders respectively.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These registers promote transparency by ensuring that when there are persons exercising control of legal persons behind the scenes, they are known to the authorities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But the usefulness of these registers depends on their accuracy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A register with inaccurate, incomplete or out-of-date information is of no use to the authorities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Those who do not update their registers in a timely manner already face penalties under the Companies Act and LLP Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These offences could include failing to maintain their registers, keep the information up to date or correct inaccurate information.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, we will make it an offence for persons to provide false or misleading information about their registers to ACRA, with a fine of up to $25,000.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will apply to persons who did not act with reasonable due diligence in ensuring the accuracy of the information that they provide to ACRA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Third, we will require companies and LLPs to verify and update their controllers' information on an annual basis.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The second set of amendments will further enhance transparency around nominee arrangements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Today, individuals who are nominee directors or shareholders are required by law to disclose their particulars and nominee status to their companies, but there is no requirement for them or their companies to share this information with ACRA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To promote even greater transparency, the Bill will require companies to provide the full information of nominee arrangements to ACRA, such as the particulars of the nominee directors and shareholders, as well as the identities of the nominators behind these nominees.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This information will only be available to ACRA and other public agencies for the enforcement of any written law.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, ACRA will make public which of the company's directors and shareholders are nominees.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, an individual's status as a nominee director will be made public, although the identity of the nominator will not be disclosed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This information will be useful to banks, CSPs and other gatekeepers who may, for instance, wish to conduct additional checks on companies with many nominee directors or shareholders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This issue cannot be single-handedly tackled by an individual stakeholder.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All stakeholders, including companies and CSPs, must each play their role in the fight against financial crime, by upholding transparency and adhering to their AML obligations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am also a Registered Qualified Individual (RQI) and my company is a Registered Filing Agent (RFA) under the ACRA Act.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Under the ACRA (Filing Agents and Qualified Individuals) Regulations, a qualified individual means either an advocate and solicitor, a public accountant registered under the Accountants Act, a member of the Institute of Singapore Chartered Accountants and so on.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Essentially, a QI must be properly qualified and be a fit and proper person before he can be a QI.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And every RFA must act by or through a registered QI.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The RFA must also attend a mandatory anti-money laundering course (MAML) or a Countering of the Financing of Terrorism (CFT) course and pass a proficiency test once in every two years.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: An RFA also needs to have a documented Internal Policy, Procedures and Control (IPPC) and an AML policy.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As an RFA, I have to attend the AML course and I have taken the proficiency test.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: An RFA helps businesses navigate the huge amount of rules and regulations relating to the operation of the company.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: According to ACRA, there are almost 600,000 businesses registered in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, RFAs are needed to help these businesses keep their statutory records and registration.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: RFAs also help to incorporate companies, draft directors and shareholders' resolutions, help file the company's annual returns and so on.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If a company wishes to increase its capital or pay dividends to its shareholders, to take a bank loan or to buy or sell property, they will need to ask an RFA to assist in the required paperwork and update their ACRA records.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If the company has given a security over its assets, the RFA will help to register a charge on the company.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is so, even if they do not file transactions on behalf of their customers with ACRA.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Second, to require companies and other business entities that carry on a business in Singapore of carrying out any "designated activity" in relation to the provision of any accounting service to be registered as CSPs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Designated activity is also defined in clause 2 of the draft Bill and would include buying and selling of real estate, managing of client money or assets.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The third objective of the Bill is to disallow a registered CSP from arranging for a person to act as a nominee director of a company, unless the CSP is satisfied that the person is fit and proper.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In determining whether the person is fit and proper, the registered CSP must take reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the person, who is a nominee director, is not disqualified from acting as a director of a company under any written law, and consider other factors prescribed in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, I believe that all parties must do their part to ensure that we deter dishonest entities from carrying out illegal activities and then laundering the illegally obtained funds through our financial system.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, Madam, I do have a few concerns.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many RFAs, now to be known as CSPs, provide critical services to many small companies and businesses to ensure that these businesses and companies do comply with the Companies Act and ACRA regulations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: These CSPs are already required to attend AML/CFT courses and to pass the mandatory test every two years.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: To impose too many requirements and to impose such high penalties of up to $100,000 fines, seem to be an excessive reaction to the current action against money launderers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They are cancelled for breaching the ACRA regulations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, Madam, there are already penalties imposed for breach of such regulations.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many RFAs typically provide company secretariat services and do not deal with huge flow of funds or monies into the companies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is unlike the banks or financial institutions, remittance companies or dealers of precious metals.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, to impose onerous requirements on the CSPs to carry out stringent customer due diligence for every company that they incorporate or service and even CDD on existing clients that they know, seems to be an overkill to me.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There will be a higher cost of compliance and this will invariably have to be passed on to the businesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And many of these businesses may be small companies which have to pay for the higher compliance costs just to run a small family business.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Surely, these banks, financial institutions or remittance companies are better placed to have stringent AML/CFT measures to stop the flow of illegal funds.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The banks and financial institutions make huge profits every year and they should bear a larger share of compliance costs to detect money laundering of illegal funds.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, the question is who is in a better position to detect money laundering activities and which entity should bear the greater part of the compliance costs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, may I urge the Minister to consider the culpability of the CSP when imposing criminal liabilities on CSPs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In this case, the question would be whether the CSP had directly facilitated the illegal flow of funds into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The criteria must be clear and easy to comply with.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Is it the duty of the registered CSP merely to ensure that a nominee director is not disqualified from acting as a director?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Or must the CSP check how many directorships is the nominee director holding?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Or are there other factors that the CSP must consider.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For example, the classic advice in AML/CFP literature is that a CSP has to carry out CDD to assess for country risk and then assess whether the customer is a politically exposed person (PEP).

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: When the customer is a PEP, then the CSP and many financial institutions would have to carry out enhanced CDD.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: PEP, in this case, would include politicians like us Members, judges, senior civil servants and so on.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For financial institutions that choose to take the easy way out, they simply reject a PEP as its customer, because they are concerned whether they will be penalised if they process wrongly someone who is a PEP as their customer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Likewise, the easy way out would be for a CSP to reject any PEP so that they do not have to take unnecessary risks.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: A former Nominated Member of Parliament (NMP) had shared with me that he had many difficulties trying to open a bank account more than 10 years after he had stepped down as an NMP.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Does ACRA check on the directorships held by any person?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Would ACRA not want to set a limit as to the number of directorship that a director can hold?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I hope the Minister can provide some clarifications on my concerns.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Over the past year, Singaporeans and many others across the world were shocked and captivated by the discovery of one of the largest money laundering operations globally happening on our shores, even as memories of the money laundering of 1MDB funds remain fresh in our minds.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As we reflect on the money laundering risks and vulnerabilities in the wake of these incidents, it is important that the reputation of our country cannot be associated with that of money laundering or "Singapore-washing", a term which I first read about in a Financial Times article from November 2022 and which was once again brought up in a Bloomberg Opinion article in June last month titled "Singapore-washing Has Hit a Wall".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We need to send a clear message to the world that we are not a haven where our financial system can be easily exploited.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When it comes to tightening our regulations, we need to err on the side of caution, even as we continually enhance our supervisory and enforcement methods, as we should.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And it is in this spirit that I wish to raise several areas of concerns and seek clarifications to the CSP Bill in this House today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One of the key areas of concern when it comes to the role of CSPs in facilitating or abetting money laundering operations is the misuse of nominee directors and the multiple layers of companies involved in money laundering networks.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This arises from the requirement for companies to have at least one director who is ordinarily resident in Singapore and, hence, a foreigner may engage CSPs to incorporate companies in Singapore while procuring nominee director services from CSPs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Companies Act requires each company to have at least one director who is ordinarily resident in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, foreigners must engage the services of CSPs to incorporate a Singapore company.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As such, a foreigner might also procure nominee director services.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In a Ministerial Statement in October last year, Minister Indranee shared that, "ACRA has been studying restrictions on directorships, both to ensure that nominee directors are fit and proper to take up the role and whether it would be useful to limit the number of nominee directorships that one can hold".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The proposal first introduced in ACRA's public consultation already provides for qualified persons to be exempt from such requirements, where qualified persons include an advocate and solicitor of the Supreme Court of Singapore, registered public accountants and members of the Institute of Singapore Chartered Accountants.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, the requirement is merely to ensure that such persons satisfy prescribed training requirements.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Today, banks have to take steps to ensure that all of its employees are regularly and appropriately trained on anti-money laundering laws and their responsibilities in combating money laundering and terrorism financing.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even property agents have to fulfil an increased number of training hours a year from October 2025 onwards.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For nominee directors, whose legal obligations are the same as other directors in discharging their duties responsibly, I do not think that minimum training requirements that were initially considered are a step too far but are, in fact, essential.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While it can be argued that it is difficult to come up with a "magic number" on the prescribed number of nominee directorships, the key here is that the proposed legislation would not have prevented non-qualified persons from taking on such nominee directorships.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: ACRA's justification in not proceeding with this proposal was that it will "enhance its supervisory and enforcement efforts on persons who hold a large number of nominee directorships and exhibit other high-risk indicators".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My question then is: does this have to be mutually exclusive?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I do hope that the Government will reconsider this training requirement proposal in due course to further strengthen our regulatory safeguards against the abuse of nominee directorships.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I have several other clarifications specific to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In what way would such guidelines and thresholds be similar or different to that of the Monetary Authority of Singapore guidelines on the fit and proper criteria?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Given that all directors, nominee or otherwise, owe a fiduciary duty to the company and have a range of other serious duties and responsibilities, it is important that we uphold high standards in determining the fit and proper criteria that should be expected of the nominee directors appointed by CSPs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Doing so will uplift the corporate governance standards of the companies on which they serve on and also complement the work of regulators in anti-money laundering efforts.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, support in the form of training and resources should also be made available to CSPs in guiding them on making such fit and proper assessments, as well as on other broader matters relating to money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Would the relevant agencies and Ministries be spearheading such training and briefings on a regular basis, to ensure that the conduct of fit and proper assessments is aligned with both legislation and the latest AML developments?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Within this sizeable group of CSPs, there could be many which are very small entities and could also be largely dominated by one or two dominant customer groups.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In such cases, the independence of judgement in the assessment of money laundering risks may be at risk of being clouded in view of commercial considerations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Are there requirements for CSPs to declare their customer concentration risks to certain groups of customers, which are ultimately related to the same beneficial ownership?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Doing so could aid ACRA in its risk assessment of the broad swathe of CSPs currently.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What is the level of intensity or duration of such prescribed courses or training?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, there could be efficiency gains for such companies and for ACRA in holding a Qualified Individual responsible for the implementation of the CSP Bill requirements.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To conclude, Mdm Deputy Speaker, while we do not want to unnecessarily stifle legitimate activities and investments, it is important that we do our utmost to prevent and detect money laundering and the use of our financial systems to facilitate illicit fund flows.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am confident that most professionals in the legal, accounting and finance functions in Singapore carry out their duties diligently and ethically and a tightening of rules and regulations could be seen as unnecessary, given that they are doing no wrong.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But when it comes to our commitment to tackling money laundering and illegal activities, we need to take a clear and strong stand, making sure that we examine the sector with a fine-tooth comb and not water down regulatory standards, so that current and prospective businesses which are legitimate can have the confidence of operating in Singapore and dealing with entities operating in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Over the past decades, Singapore has emerged as a global financial centre.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This episode occurred despite our regular reviews of our AML strategy, such as the 2022 requirement for companies to maintain registers of nominee shareholders and directors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Bad actors will continue to find their ways to mask their activities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As Singapore strives to maintain its reputation as an open and transparent financial hub, stringent legislation at all levels is necessary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must protect our financial sector from illicit activities and strengthen global investor confidence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It aims to strengthen the regulatory regime governing CSPs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It ensures they rigorously adhere to AML protocols and align with international standards set by bodies, such as the Financial Action Task Force (FATF).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: CSPs can act as key gatekeepers against money laundering, serving as part of our first line of defence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Under the proposed Bill, CSPs can only conduct business if they are registered for the type of corporate service they provide.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Section 9 outlines the Registrar's responsibilities, including the mandate to refuse applications or renewals under specific circumstances.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To enhance the Bill's effectiveness against money laundering, we should consider extending this mandatory "cooling-off" period beyond two years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The duration of this period should also differ, based on the severity of the non-compliance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This will underscore the seriousness of regulatory compliance and act as a stringent deterrent against non-compliance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Bill also mandates CSPs and qualified individuals to complete prescribed courses or training related to Customer Due Diligence (CDD) requirements and AML best practices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Sufficient time should be provided for CSPs to meet such requirements.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement, through NTUC Learning Hub, is ready to partner ACRA and the Ministry to deliver these courses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Ministry should also consider providing training subsidies to facilitate broader access and affordability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Section 8(3) grants the Registrar discretion to impose different conditions on registered CSPs based on various classes or circumstances.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I agree that tailored conditions would ensure robust AML safeguards while not causing unnecessary compliance costs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Clarification is needed, however, on what are these circumstances that would justify differing conditions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This would better guide companies in deciding whether they are required to register as a CSP and, as for the existing CSPs, how could they prepare to meet escalated conditions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Certainly, for CSPs with international operations and, thus, facing heightened risks in managing international transactions, enhanced requirements must be imposed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Section 17 introduces stringent measures to combat money laundering, proliferation financing and terrorism financing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Registered CSPs must perform comprehensive CDD in various crucial circumstances: before providing any corporate service, upon suspicion of illicit activities and when there is reason to doubt previous CDD findings.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A critical requirement is conducting CDD based on previous findings, necessitating CSPs to reassess and update their CDD measures periodically.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can I seek clarification on whether there will be a prescribed look-back period or if CSPs must undertake a full review of their current CDD for all existing customers?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is essential to strike a balance that ensures AML compliance while considering the operational feasibility for CSPs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: By tightening the regulatory oversight of CSPs, we reaffirm our commitment to global leadership in combating financial crime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As we move forward, let us remember: "The price of freedom from financial crime is eternal vigilance." Let us ensure Singapore retains its position as a trusted financial hub in the international space.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I will refer to these as AML/CFT/PF, for short.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While I support this Bill, I seek seven clarifications from the Minister.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My first few clarifications relate to how the proposed Bill will apply to law firms, especially when they provide tax-related legal services.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Clause 3(1) of the Bill includes in its definition of "taxation services" four different types of services namely – the ensuring of compliance by an entity with written law relating to tax in the course of preparing tax returns, the making of tax calculations for the purpose of preparing accounting entries for an entity's financial statements, the provision of advice in relation to tax and tax planning; and the provision of assistance in the resolution of tax disputes.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If these services are rendered in relation to certain "designated activities" they then become "corporate services" which are within the scope of the new Bill.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Certain tax provisions for example, section 34A and section 34AA of the Income Tax Act 1947 relating to the taxation of financial instruments, directly import the application of financial reporting standards, such as FRS 39 and FRS 109, into tax law.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While financial accounting rules are generally not definitive of tax positions, the outlook may be different where tax legislation directly refers to financial reporting standards.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, in other words, if a tax lawyer was looking to advise on section 34A or section 34AA of the Income Tax Act, he or she would necessarily have to refer to and apply financial reporting standards, as well as the law.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If for example, a tax lawyer is engaged to work on a matter involving the application of section 34AA of the Income Tax Act, and this arises in the wider context of a corporate restructuring exercise that his or her firm is working on and the deal involves "the buying and selling of business entities" what would the relevant treatment be?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Would this then result in the law firm's tax work being covered by the Bill because some "accounting or related skill" is necessarily being applied?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Or is it the case that the standard of accounting skill involved has to be something higher?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Does it have to be equivalent to that of a professional practising accountant, before regulation under the Bill is triggered?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I am aware that the term "accounting or related skill" is currently found in the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (Prescribed Accounting Services and Conditions) Regulations 2023.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These regulations apply to situations where a non-accounting entity voluntarily wishes to apply to ACRA to be described as a "Chartered Accountant of Singapore".

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This might suggest that a high standard of accounting skill, equivalent to that of a professional practising accountant, must be involved before the Bill is triggered for any "taxation services".

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: However, this is not immediately apparent from the plain wording of the proposed Bill.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To this end, I would like to refer to CDD recommendation No 22 issued by FATF for designated non-financial businesses and professions such as lawyers and accountants.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This recommendation adopts very similar language to that of the proposed Bill, and it is recognised there that representing clients in disputes and mediations, as well as the provision of advisory services on regulations, are not specified activities covered by FATF's CDD requirements.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill's definition of "designated activities" draws from FATF's standards and it is unclear when some of the "accounting services" defined at clause 3(1) of the Bill would as a matter of practical effect, be covered as "designated activities".

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This includes matters such as tax disputes work and tax advisory work, as well as other types of accounting work such as "internal audit work".

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is fundamentally something that is not transactionally-oriented as a service.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, does the link to "transactional" activity unnecessarily narrow down the scope of the proposed Bill?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It would be useful if the Government could comment on this point and provide some guidance on the intended interaction between the terms defined as "accounting services" and "designated activities" for the purposes of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, taxation services in themselves are currently not covered by any CDD regulations.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill proposes to remedy this, but only to the extent that it is done as a part of providing "accounting services".

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate that the Government's intention may be to align the scope of regulation with the requirements of FATF and to go no further.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Fourthly, further to clause 7(2) of the Bill, accounting firms will automatically be treated as registered for the purposes of the new proposed law.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There is however no similar carve-out for law firms.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In my view, it would be more correct in principle to completely exclude practising lawyers from the Bill, in order to avoid law practices from being subject to two sets of overlapping AML/CFT/PF obligations.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Being subject to overlapping but similar CDD regimes is not ideal.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My fifth and sixth clarifications relate to clause 29 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is also unclear as to what will constitute "action towards creating and maintaining a corporate culture that does not direct, encourage, tolerate or lead to non-compliance" under the new rules.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Is the Minister able to clarify if further guidance will be issued on these points and on whether regulated corporate service providers will be assisted with the training and tools necessary to support their own compliance with these new rules?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My last clarification has to do with future plans by the Government in the AML/CFT/PF regulatory space.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In recent times, our headlines have been marred by high-profile cases of money laundering.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is alongside a worrying trend in cybercrime.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These incidents are not just isolated events; they are symptomatic of a larger issue that threatens the very fabric and integrity of our economy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These Bills are tabled with the presumption that they will serve as a bulwark against the misuse of our financial system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While the intentions of the Bills are clear, I have several clarifications.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mdm Deputy Speaker, how will the Bills concretely improve transparency and accountability within CSPs, LLPs and all relevant business and companies?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mandating the registration of CSPs is a commendable move to maintain industry standards.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, it is imperative that these criteria emphasise not just qualifications, but also the reliability and integrity of the entities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on the mechanisms that will be employed to vet and verify the qualifications of CSPs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What mechanisms are in place to ensure that the information provided by company controllers is accurate and up-todate?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Foreign entities are expected to have the same standard as local entities when it comes to registering their nominee directors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will ACRA ensure that such registration is correct regarding foreign entities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How have insights from these cases shaped the registration and information-sharing criteria?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Given that financial crime prevention is one of the key goals, what specific outcomes are expected in this regard?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the success of these measures be quantified and evaluated?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mdm Deputy Speaker, for these Bills to be truly effective, awareness and enforcement are necessary to ensure regulatory compliance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is imperative that the regulatory actions and enforcement mechanisms outlined are not only stringent but also practical and implementable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the enforcement mechanisms outlined in the Bills discourage malpractice among service providers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What steps will be taken to monitor and warrant compliance?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government also provide more details on the prescribed frequency and form of notifications to registrable controllers to ensure ample notice and awareness?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mdm Deputy Speaker, it is important to strike a balancing act between transparency and data protection.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In enhancing transparency, how does the CLLP Bill balance the need for openness with the protection of sensitive information?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What measures are in place to prevent unauthorised access to the registers of nominee directors and controllers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mdm Deputy Speaker, can the Minister elaborate on mechanisms in place for appeals and legal protections?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The inclusion of an appeal process for service providers to challenge decisions made by the Registrar is commendable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It establishes a robust system for review and ensures that fairness and due process are upheld.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the CSP Bill ensure that the appeals process upholds the principles of fairness and transparency?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this connection, clause 23(2) of the CSP Bill states that a person who appeals the decision of the Registrar must specify the grounds of appeal.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, it is unclear if the Registrar will provide the grounds of the Registrar’s decision.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The lack thereof may hinder the said person from submitting substantive grounds of appeal.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fifth, Mdm Deputy Speaker, we must comprehend the extent of these Bills' impact on businesses and proactively provide support to alleviate any foreseeable negative consequences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In recent months, we have seen a surge in new bills and policies introduced in response to the increase in financial crimes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, there is a concern that businesses may struggle to keep pace with these rapid changes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Providing a clear implementation timeline empowers companies to proactively plan and adapt to the new requirements of the Bills.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Registrar ensure timely updates and accuracy in the registers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What support or guidance will be available to companies, especially small and medium enterprises, as they adapt to the new regulatory framework?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there provisions in the CLLP Bill to assist businesses to transit to the new regulatory framework, such as training or grants?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Sixth, Mdm Deputy Speaker, we must remain cognisant of our duty to serve the public interest without causing undue disruption.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What provisions are in place to ensure that the day-to-day function of corporations or individuals who wish to incorporate new corporate entities are not disproportionately inconvenienced by these new regulations, which may reduce the number of CSPs in the short term?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These cases have imparted valuable lessons, emphasising the pivotal role of CSPs in our business ecosystem and their inadvertent link to money laundering activities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: CSPs may be used, on purpose or heedlessly, to create complex corporate structures that can obscure the true ownership and control of assets.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This makes it difficult to trace illicit funds.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is important for CSPs to maintain a high standard of compliance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is to prevent their services from being misused for money laundering or other illicit financial activities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We will also have a better picture of who are behind companies to ensure greater accountability and ease for culpability, should there be any illicit activities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These Bills are Singapore's commitment to ensure that companies operate within a framework that is not just stringent but also just.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Increased trust and transparency are the cornerstones upon which businesses thrive and the two Bills are a beacon that signals to the world that Singapore is synonymous with integrity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are a crucial step in safeguarding Singapore's financial system against misuse and in preserving the sanctity of our economic sovereignty.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: In parallel with Singapore's rapid development as a financial centre, the CSP sector have seen significant growth, providing a wide range of fiduciary and administrative services to corporates, investment managers and high-net-worth individuals.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: By imposing stricter compliance requirements and heavier penalties, the Bills seek to ensure that CSPs uphold rigorous anti-money laundering standards.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: The Bill also aims to prevent money laundering and the financing of terrorism by imposing stringent requirements on CSPs.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: The legislation will also provide training opportunities for staff employed in the sector, to help them keep up-to-date with the latest developments in the industry and ensure they do not fall short of the law in their work.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: The Bill also establishes the role of the Registrar of CSPs and details registration processes, renewal requirements and obligations of registered providers.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: However, I believe this Bill could also bring about challenges to businesses and owners.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: To comply, companies in this sector need to prepare extensive documentation to register as CSPs or to ensure their own service providers are properly registered.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: These new administrative tasks demand considerable effort and resources from small businesses, diverting attention from other critical activities.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: This reallocation of resources, in terms of time and people and system upgrades to meet new standards, can cause temporary interruptions in service delivery.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: In my view, smaller, specialised CSPs will continue to play an important role in this sector.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: We just need to ensure we do not stifle growth of this very important sector by bringing about major changes at too rapid a pace.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
text: Understanding these aspects ensures that applicants can comply effectively with the registration process quickly, avoiding any delays or rejections.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarifications to raise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the duties imposed on CSPs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on the extent of reasonable steps that must be taken?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also provide examples of the factors which will be prescribed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the public consultation, respondents asked whether these requirements apply retrospectively to nominee directors' appointments made before the CSP Bill might come into force.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOF and ACRA clarified that this requirement will not apply retrospectively.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding that the requirement will not apply retrospectively, in the event that a CSP discovers that an existing nominee director is not considered a fit and proper person based on any prescribed factors, can the Minister clarify what the CSP will be obliged to do in this situation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the public consultation, MOF and ACRA also clarified that the obligation to ensure that a nominee director is fit and proper is an ongoing one.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister provide further guidance on the steps that a CSP must take to discharge this ongoing obligation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on CSPs' duties to perform customer due diligence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 17(1) requires a CSP to perform customer due diligence measures in certain circumstances.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, under section 17(3), a CSP may choose not to perform or complete any customer due diligence measure, if the CSP has reason to suspect that the transaction relates to money laundering, proliferation financing or terrorism financing and performing the measures will tip-off the customer or any person.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, under section 17(4), if a CSP is unable or chooses not to complete any customer due diligence measure, the CSP must decline to provide or terminate ongoing corporate services.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the reason for not performing or completing any customer due diligence measure is because doing so will tip the customer off, the CSP's refusal to provide or termination of corporate services may also risk tipping-off any person.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify how CSP should proceed in refusing to provide or terminating its services, if it is concerned about the risk of tipping-off any person?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final clarification is on regulatory breaches.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify whether the provisions on regulatory breaches gives the Registrar the power to treat each day of continuing regulatory breaches as fresh instances of contravention or non-compliance which can be separately penalised?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under sections 18(4)(b)(iii) and 20(4)(b)(iii), the Registrar may determine that there was a contravention or non-compliance of regulation and decide not to take regulatory action.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify whether the CSP or individual involved will be informed that the Registrar determined that there was a contravention or non-compliance, and decided not to take regulatory action?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also clarify whether the Registrar can take into account this earlier determination that there was a contravention or non-compliance as an antecedent if the CSP or individual later commits an offence or regulatory breach?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also share what other implications will arise from the Registrar determining that there was a contravention or non-compliance, even if no regulatory action is taken?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, will this record be considered in any future application by the CSP or individual?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If there are potential future implications from the Registrar's determination that there was a contravention or non-compliance, even if no action is taken, the CSP or individual should be informed of the determination, so that they can decide whether to challenge the determination.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under section 23(1), any regulatory action by the Registrar can be appealed to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It does not appear that a determination of contravention or non-compliance can be appealed against.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If a determination of contravention or non-compliance may have future implications, even when no regulatory action was taken, how can the CSP or individual challenge the Registrar's determination?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Being an open economy and a leading global financial centre, Singapore is exposed to significant money laundering risks.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A Bloomberg article, dated 17 June, coined the term "Singapore-washing".

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These two Bills are timely and will plug the loopholes being exploited.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   I would like to seek clarifications regarding some of the clauses in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will the proposed registration requirements ensure that all CSPs comply effectively with Anti-Money Laundering, Combating the Financing of Terrorism and Proliferation Finance regulations?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What mechanisms will be put in place to monitor compliance and prevent regulatory overlaps or impose excessive burdens on CSPs?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Ministry share more information about its measures to establish a robust monitoring and evaluation framework to assess the effectiveness of the new requirements while minimising regulatory burdens? : Clauses 3 and 7 require the inclusion of companies which carry out any designated activities, in relation to the provision of any accounting service as registered CSPs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What specific risks have been identified that justify extending AML/CFT/PF requirements to all accounting service providers and how will ACRA ensure that these providers are adequately prepared to comply with these new regulations?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Is ACRA able to ensure that the CSPs employ qualified accounting professionals to provide accounting and bookkeeping services to companies incorporated in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The unqualified professionals do not answer to any accountancy body, like ISCA or CPA Australia.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I recommend that targeted training and resources be provided to ensure that they understand and comply with the new requirements while minimising disruptions to their operations.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will this impact the willingness of individuals to take on these roles and what safeguards will be in place to protect against undue penalties?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, would the Ministry provide a mechanism for senior management to appeal decisions or demonstrate due diligence to avoid unjust penalties?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Organisations, like ISCA, also run programmes to help new and aspiring directors to acquire new knowledge, build competencies and attain board readiness as well as for existing directors to keep themselves abreast of developments in the corporate governance space.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I suggest that the Ministry develop a standardised set of criteria and a verification process, including access to relevant databases, that CSPs can use to assess the fitness of nominee directors.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This process should be transparent and ensure that CSPs can perform these checks efficiently and effectively.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: About the introduction of clause 17 to detect and prevent the proliferation financing of weapons of mass destruction (WMDs), how will the requirement for CSPs to comply with this new regulation be integrated with existing AML/CFT frameworks and what specific challenges might CSPs face in meeting these new obligations?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I propose that the Ministry align the new requirements with existing AML/CFT frameworks to ensure consistency and avoid duplicative efforts.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: CSPs should be provided with clear guidelines and examples of best practices for detecting and preventing PF and offered regular training sessions to help them stay informed of evolving threats and compliance strategies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Implement the new regulations in phases, starting with high-risk CSPs and gradually include other entities.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This approach allows for adjustments based on feedback and ensures that all entities have adequate time to comply.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Provide comprehensive training programmes and support resources for CSPs to help them understand and comply with the new requirements.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This includes workshops, online courses and access to advisory services.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It will be better if additional training grants can be provided to these CSPs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Establish a robust monitoring system to track compliance and gather feedback from CSPs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government can use this feedback to refine regulations and support mechanisms, ensuring that they are effective and not overly burdensome.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Ensure that penalties for non-compliance are proportionate to the severity of the breach.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Implement a clear distinction between minor infractions and serious violations, with appropriate penalties for each category.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Maintain transparent communication with CSPs about the rationale for the new requirements, the expected benefits and the processes involved.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Regular updates and open channels for feedback will help build trust and compliance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I just want to emphasise, as I did to my opening speech, that the proposals in the Bills were actually already in development even before the case was uncovered.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the amendments do not stem from nor are they solely in response to that particular case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But that said, we refined certain proposals to incorporate the insights gleaned from the ongoing Inter-Ministerial Committee as well as lessons learnt from the case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For instance, as part of the CLLP Bill, we are strengthening upstream controls and corporate transparency by ensuring that persons exercising control of legal persons behind-the-scenes, or registrable controllers in short, are identified at the point of incorporation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Such information would be immediately available to relevant authorities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With this context, let me now address clarifications on the Corporate Service Providers Bill or CSP Bill, before moving on to the Companies and Limited Liability Partnerships (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, on the CSP Bill, Members raised queries around three main themes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, the registration criteria and obligations of CSPs; second, nominee directors; and third, penalties and avenue for appeals, which I will address in turn.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Neil Parekh, Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Desmond Choo asked about the criteria to register as a CSP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These requirements and mechanisms to register as a CSP are similar to our existing regulatory regime for Registered Filing Agents or RFAs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Key appointment holders and RQIs will be subjected to screening checks by ACRA and the CSP must also complete a prescribed AML/CFT course before their application for registration will be considered.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: More details of the registration requirements for CSPs can be found at clauses 8 and 9 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Any conditions on registration will be published by ACRA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Don Wee asked about the requirement for accounting service providers to be registered as CSPs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Examples of designated activities include, carrying out transactions for a customer relating to the management of client monies and bank accounts and the buying or selling of real estate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For accounting entities that are already registered with ACRA under the Accountants Act, they do not need to apply to ACRA to be separately registered as CSPs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They will be automatically be registered as CSPs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To Ms Usha Chandradas' queries, other professionals, like practising lawyers and law firms who provide legal services on tax matters, do not need to be registered with ACRA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They are actually heavily-regulated, but that is under a separate legislation and regime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This Bill is also not intended to cover other services, such as taxation services provided by non-accountants and the art market.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan, Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Neil Parekh and Mr Louis Ng inquired on the obligations of CSPs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The measures in this Bill do not fundamentally affect CSPs' obligations insofar as customer due diligence and AML/CFT checks are concerned.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They reinforce the existing measures that the industry is already familiar with.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Don Wee also asked about the new requirement for CSPs to detect and prevent the proliferation financing of WMDs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These duties would be similar to the existing duties of CSPs to counter money laundering and the financing of terrorism.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: CSPs will be required to screen against sources of information, like the relevant regulations under the United Nations Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The sources of information will be prescribed in subsidiary legislation and ACRA will also publish guidelines to raise the industry's awareness and understanding of proliferation financing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We do not expect this requirement to significantly increase the CSPs' compliance obligations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Don Wee and Mr Yip Hon Weng also asked how the requirements in this Bill will be enforced to ensure that CSPs comply with their obligations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Today, ACRA already conducts regular inspections to ensure CSPs comply with their anti-money laundering obligations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: During these inspections, ACRA will assess, among other things, the CSPs' approach to assessing money laundering or terrorism financing risks; obtaining of beneficial ownership information; record-keeping; and customer due diligence procedures.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If CSPs are found to violate or be negligent in any of their obligations, they could be subject to fines and regulatory action from ACRA, including cancellation of their registration as a CSP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Desmond Choo referred to this as the two-year "cooling off" period and suggested to extend its duration.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: An entity or individual may reapply to ACRA after two years, but this does not mean that their registration would necessarily be successful.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: ACRA will subject all applications received after the "cooling off" period to higher scrutiny.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In instances where applicants did not meet the requirements, such as the "fit and proper" criteria, ACRA will not approve their re-registration, even after two years.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Besides enforcement, ACRA also publishes guidance and participates in industry fora to share best practices and raise awareness, so as to better support the sector in discharging its AML/CFT obligations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Don Wee, Mr Louis Ng and Mr Lim Biow Chuan sought clarifications on the requirement for CSPs to be satisfied that the individuals they arrange to act as nominee directors are "fit and proper".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: ACRA will also provide additional guidance on how CSPs can fulfil this obligation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, CSPs must also exercise their professional judgement when making arrangements for individuals to be nominee directors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Ng also asked how CSPs should discharge this ongoing obligation to ensure that nominee directors are "fit and proper".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Once an individual is appointed as a nominee director, it is the company's obligation, under the Companies Act, to ensure that their directors, nominee or otherwise, remain "fit and proper".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, if the CSP has reasons to believe that its appointed nominee director is no longer "fit and proper", after the appointment, it should also take appropriate action, such as informing the company involved to replace the individual concerned.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Again, I would like to repeat the general principle from my opening speech, which is that ultimately, each CSP must exercise professionalism and undertake responsibility for its actions or lack thereof.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Chua had asked about the issue of whether or not we should have a regime where we specify the number of nominee directors or have a threshold of nominee directors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On this, it was previously mentioned that ACRA was studying if it would be useful to limit the number of nominee directorships that one can hold.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This was because prescribing the number of nominee directorships that an individual can hold, could be a blunt tool that is unnecessarily restrictive.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It would make it difficult for individuals who are capable of fulfilling their obligations, despite holding more than the prescribed number and who may have legitimate reasons for holding multiple nominee directorships.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At the same time, bad actors could always find ways to get around the prescribed number.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It could also inadvertently raise the cost of doing business as companies may need to source from more individuals to fulfill this requirement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that said, we still remain committed to addressing this issue.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Earlier, I had spoken about two new measures that we are introducing: the requirement for CSPs to arrange for the appointment of individuals as nominee directors by way of business and for the CSPs to ensure that the nominee directors appointed through them are fit and proper.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Beyond these legislative amendments, ACRA has also stepped up their supervisory and enforcement efforts for those who hold a large number of nominee directorships and exhibit other high-risk indicators and ACRA will continue to do so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Moving on to the third bucket of queries around penalties and avenues for legal protection.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Wee and Mr Lim asked about the criminal liability that will be imposed on registered CSPs and their senior management for breaching their obligations to combat financial crime and the quantum of the fines.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Imposing criminal liability for breaches relating to anti-money laundering obligations is consistent with the legislation governing other gatekeepers in Singapore, and better reflects the serious nature of the breaches.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Such liabilities would be adjudicated and determined by the Courts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To Mr Lim’s suggestion for the banks to be held accountable for money laundering breaches rather than CSPs, I would say that guarding against money laundering is a whole-of-society effort and the CSPs must play their part.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I agree that banks are a critical gatekeeper, and they do have onerous obligations and there are existing AML regulations in place for banks.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Banks will similarly face sanctions, including fines, if they breach any obligations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is a maximum quantum and the actual amount of fine meted out would depend on the facts of each case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To Mr Wee's suggestion to distinguish between minor compliance issues and serious breaches, this has and will remain in place as ACRA will still be able to take regulatory action for breaches of a less serious nature.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On a related note, Ms Chandradas asked how a corporation's "state of mind" will be proven under clause 29 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will depend on the wording of the particular offence and the general principles of criminal law.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As for avenues for legal protection and appeals, if a CSP is found to have contravened any of their obligations, ACRA will first inform the CSP of the contravention, regardless of whether there is any regulatory action against the CSP.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In cases where ACRA intends to take regulatory action, a "show cause" letter will be sent to the CSP, setting out the contraventions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The CSP will then have the opportunity to make written representations to ACRA to explain as it were.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is provided for in clause 22 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Yip asked about the measures that are implemented to ensure data accuracy of our various corporate registers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First and foremost, it is the responsibility of companies to ensure that the information they maintain in their registers is accurate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: While we understand that companies depend on the information provided to them from their controllers or nominee directors, the companies will be responsible for sending notices to their controllers annually to ensure that the information is kept up to date.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition, ACRA leverages data analytics and conducts ongoing inspections to verify that the information contained in the various registers is accurate and up to date.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The measures and underlying principles broadly apply to both local and foreign companies that are required to maintain the registers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As Mr Yip mentioned, the data that is contained in these registers is of a sensitive nature and must be safeguarded appropriately.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hence, it is critical to strike the right balance between the need for transparency and data protection.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is why we always monitor this trade off and are prepared to introduce changes where necessary.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, we have introduced a new framework for differentiated information disclosure, not in this Bill but in the ACRA (Registry and Regulatory Enhancements) Bill that was just read earlier.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The framework will protect confidentiality of personal information by limiting public access, while still allowing selected, specified parties to access the information to fulfil their legal obligations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On ease of doing business, I also agree with Mr Yip, Mr Wee and Mr Parekh about the need to balance between compliance cost, ease of doing business and the extent of controls and safeguards to combat financial crime.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is why we have consulted stakeholders extensively and carefully calibrated the requirements in both Bills to ensure that on one hand, appropriate measures can be taken in relation to those who breach their obligations, while on the other hand, we continue to ensure that Singapore remains open and friendly to legitimate businesses, and the cost of compliance remains manageable.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The requirements in the Bill are existing best practices that CSPs should already be adopting.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition, we have taken steps to ensure that the transition will be as seamless as possible.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: ACRA will communicate the effective date of commencement in advance, provide the necessary support, such as guidance, and sufficient lead time for CSPs to implement the necessary changes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Similarly, for the registers-related requirements, ACRA will notify companies ahead of time of the timeline and the means to file the necessary information.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I also agree with Mr Choo and Ms Chandradas on the necessity of training.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will explore working with the relevant stakeholders, such as the professional bodies and the labour union, to develop training courses to support individuals in acquiring the necessary skills to fulfil the obligations in these Bills.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think there were a couple of other queries which Mr Louis Chua had raised.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He had asked, I think, whether in a situation where you have a group of companies connected to each other providing different corporate services to the same set of clients, whether it is necessary for them to have duplicate registration and whether there will be duplicate, I think – there will be duplication in maintaining the due diligence for the AML risk.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first thing to understand is that, if it is different companies providing different corporate services, the different entities each must comply and register.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I mean, it depends on the nature of what they are doing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But if you are an entity that is providing corporate services and you have two entities, then it has to be two registrations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If you are providing different services, you still have to register separately.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is also because they would be providing different services, which are associated with different risk.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And I think he asked about the definition of key appointment holders under the Act.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There is a definition under the CSP Act of key appointment holders.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That would be under section 2, the general interpretation section and it defines "key appointment holders", in relation to any person.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, a key appointment holder means this in relation to any of the following persons: where X is a sole proprietorship, then the sole proprietor is the key appointment holder.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
